title: Postgres EXPLAIN ANALYZE: Reading the Planner's Mind
summary: A dense field guide to Postgres query plans — how to read EXPLAIN ANALYZE output, every scan and join strategy, where costs and row estimates come from, and how to diagnose the moments the planner guesses wrong.

chapters.title: EXPLAIN Fundamentals: Reading the Output
points: EXPLAIN shows the planner's chosen plan without running it; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query and reports real timings
Plans are trees of nodes; output is indented, children below parents, and execution flows bottom-up (leaves feed parents)
Read a plan inside-out: the most indented node runs first, the top node returns the final rows
Node line anatomy: `Seq Scan on orders (cost=0.00..18334.00 rows=1000000 width=33)`
cost=startup..total — startup is cost before first row emitted, total is cost to return all rows
rows = estimated row count for THAT node, width = estimated average bytes per row
With ANALYZE you also get `(actual time=0.015..85.2 rows=1000000 loops=3)` — real startup ms, total ms, real rows, and loop count
CRITICAL: actual rows and actual time are PER LOOP averages — multiply by loops for the true total
`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` adds shared hit/read/dirtied/written — the single most useful extra flag
Other options: VERBOSE (output columns, schema-qualified names), SETTINGS (non-default GUCs), WAL, TIMING OFF, FORMAT JSON|YAML|TEXT
`Planning Time` vs `Execution Time` — a 3ms plan for a 2ms query means the planning itself is the bottleneck
ANALYZE runs the query for real: wrap writes in `BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE UPDATE ...; ROLLBACK;`
`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF)` when per-node timing overhead (gettimeofday) distorts a fast query
Filter vs Index Cond vs Recheck Cond: Filter runs after rows are fetched, Index Cond narrows inside the index
`Rows Removed by Filter: 998000` is a red flag — you read a million rows to keep two thousand

chapters.title: Scan Types: Getting Rows Off Disk
points: Seq Scan — reads every page of the table in physical order; cheapest per page, fine when selectivity is low (>5-10% of table)
Index Scan — walks the index, then does a random heap fetch per match; good for high selectivity and when you need ordered output
Index Only Scan — answers entirely from the index; requires all referenced columns in the index AND a visible-enough visibility map
`Heap Fetches: N` on an Index Only Scan — nonzero means the visibility map is stale; VACUUM to drop it toward zero
Bitmap Heap Scan + Bitmap Index Scan — builds a bitmap of matching TIDs, sorts it, then reads the heap in physical order
Bitmap scan wins in the middle ground: too many rows for random index fetches, too few to justify reading the whole table
`Recheck Cond` appears because the bitmap may go lossy (page-level, not tuple-level) once work_mem fills
`Heap Blocks: exact=1204 lossy=8891` — lossy blocks mean work_mem was too small and every tuple on those pages is rechecked
BitmapAnd / BitmapOr — combine several indexes for one query; why multiple single-column indexes can beat one composite
TID Scan — direct fetch by ctid, e.g. `WHERE ctid = '(0,1)'`
Function Scan, Values Scan, Result — set-returning functions, VALUES lists, and constant-only nodes
CTE Scan and Subquery Scan — materialized intermediate result sets
Covering index syntax: `CREATE INDEX ... ON t (a, b) INCLUDE (c)` to enable Index Only Scan without widening the key
Index type matters: B-tree for =/</>/BETWEEN/prefix LIKE, GIN for arrays and full text, GiST for ranges and geometry, BRIN for huge naturally-ordered tables
A Seq Scan is not automatically a bug — on a 200-row table it beats every index

chapters.title: Join Strategies: Nested Loop, Hash, Merge
points: Nested Loop — for each outer row, probe the inner side; cost roughly outer_rows × inner_cost
Nested Loop is optimal when the outer side is tiny and the inner side has an index on the join key
A Nested Loop with a Seq Scan on the inner side and a large outer side is a classic disaster: O(N×M)
Hash Join — builds a hash table from the smaller side (`Hash` node), then probes it while streaming the other side
`Buckets: 8192 Batches: 1 Memory Usage: 4096kB` — Batches > 1 means the hash spilled to disk; raise work_mem
Hash Join only supports equality conditions (=), never < or >, never non-equijoins
Merge Join — sorts both inputs on the join key, then walks them in lockstep like a zipper
Merge Join is nearly free when both sides already arrive sorted (index order); brutal when it must Sort a huge input
Join order matters as much as join method — the planner reorders joins, but only within its search limits
Inner side of a Nested Loop shows `loops=N` — that is where the real cost hides
Parameterized (dependent) inner scans: `Index Cond: (o.customer_id = c.id)` means the inner index scan uses the outer row's value
Semi Join (EXISTS / IN) stops at the first inner match; Anti Join (NOT EXISTS) emits outer rows with no match
LEFT JOIN forces a join direction — the nullable side must be the inner side, restricting the planner's options
Memoize node caches inner-side results across loops when join keys repeat — turns a repeated Nested Loop probe into a lookup
Rule of thumb: small×indexed = Nested Loop, big×big equality = Hash, both pre-sorted = Merge

chapters.title: Cost Estimates: Where the Numbers Come From
points: Cost is a unitless abstract number, not milliseconds — comparable only between plans for the same query
seq_page_cost = 1.0 is the unit everything else is measured against
random_page_cost = 4.0 by default — models a spinning disk; set to 1.1 for SSD/NVMe so index scans stop looking overpriced
cpu_tuple_cost = 0.01, cpu_index_tuple_cost = 0.005, cpu_operator_cost = 0.0025
Seq Scan cost = (pages × seq_page_cost) + (rows × cpu_tuple_cost) — worked example on a 10k-page, 1M-row table
effective_cache_size (default 4GB) does NOT allocate memory; it tells the planner how much of the table is likely already cached
Startup cost is nonzero for blocking nodes (Sort, Hash, aggregation) — they must consume all input before emitting a row
LIMIT interacts with startup cost: a plan with a high total cost but zero startup can win under LIMIT 10
parallel_setup_cost (1000) and parallel_tuple_cost (0.1) explain why small queries never go parallel
The planner picks the lowest total cost path — or lowest startup path when a cursor or LIMIT is in play
Costs are additive up the tree: a parent's total includes all its children
JIT kicks in above jit_above_cost (100000) — can add 20ms of compile time to a query that runs in 5ms
Tune costs as a set, not one at a time; random_page_cost and effective_cache_size are the two that move real workloads
Never compare costs across different queries or different tables — they are only ordinally meaningful within one search

chapters.title: Statistics: How the Planner Guesses Row Counts
points: ANALYZE (the command, not the EXPLAIN option) samples the table and stores stats in pg_statistic, readable via pg_stats
default_statistics_target = 100 — the planner samples about 300 × target = 30,000 rows per table
pg_stats columns: null_frac, avg_width, n_distinct, most_common_vals, most_common_freqs, histogram_bounds, correlation
MCV list holds the most common values and their frequencies — exact selectivity for skewed values
Histogram buckets cover everything outside the MCV list, each holding roughly equal row counts
n_distinct negative means a ratio: -1 = every value unique, -0.5 = each value appears twice
correlation near 1.0 or -1.0 means physical order tracks logical order — makes index scans much cheaper
Selectivity for `col = 'x'`: MCV frequency if listed, else (1 - sum(mcv_freqs) - null_frac) / (n_distinct - mcv_count)
Autovacuum triggers ANALYZE at autovacuum_analyze_threshold (50) + 0.1 × reltuples changed rows
Raise per-column detail: `ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c SET STATISTICS 1000;` then re-ANALYZE
Extended statistics fix correlated columns: `CREATE STATISTICS s (dependencies, ndistinct, mcv) ON city, state FROM addr;`
Without extended stats the planner multiplies selectivities as if columns are independent — city='Paris' AND country='France' underestimates badly
Expression indexes get their own stats; a bare `WHERE lower(email) = ...` without one falls back to a 0.5% default guess
Fixed fallback constants when stats are missing: 0.5% for equality, 33% for inequality range
A freshly restored dump or a just-bulk-loaded table has no stats at all — ANALYZE before benchmarking

chapters.title: Parallelism, Sorts, and Aggregates
points: Gather node collects rows from parallel workers; `Workers Planned: 4 Workers Launched: 2` means the pool ran out
Gather Merge preserves sort order from workers; Gather does not
Parallel Seq Scan divides pages among workers — actual rows shown are per-worker, so leader + workers sum to the total
max_parallel_workers_per_gather (default 2) caps workers per Gather; max_worker_processes caps the whole cluster
Table must exceed min_parallel_table_scan_size (8MB) before parallelism is even considered
Sort node reports `Sort Method: quicksort Memory: 25kB` or `external merge Disk: 24000kB` — Disk means work_mem was exceeded
Sort keys, top-N heapsort for `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n`, and why that avoids sorting the full set
HashAggregate — builds a hash table of groups; unordered output, fast, but memory-hungry
GroupAggregate — requires sorted input, streams groups, constant memory
Postgres 13+ HashAggregate can spill to disk instead of blowing up: `Disk Usage: 12000kB`
Incremental Sort — reuses a partial index ordering, sorting only within groups of already-ordered prefix columns
Materialize node caches a subplan's rows so an inner side can be rescanned without re-running
WindowAgg for window functions; Unique for DISTINCT on sorted input
work_mem is per sort/hash node per worker — a 10-node parallel plan can multiply it far past what you budgeted
Append vs Merge Append for partitions and UNION ALL; `Subplans Removed: 7` proves partition pruning worked

chapters.title: When the Planner Goes Wrong
points: The core diagnostic: compare estimated `rows=` against `actual rows=` at every node, starting from the leaves
Estimation error compounds upward — a 10× error at a leaf becomes a 1000× error three joins up
Underestimate signature: planner picks Nested Loop expecting 5 rows, gets 500,000, and the query hangs
Overestimate signature: planner picks Hash Join and a full Seq Scan when a cheap Index Scan would have done
Stale statistics — the most common root cause; check `last_analyze` and `last_autoanalyze` in pg_stat_user_tables
Correlated columns without extended statistics — the independence assumption multiplies selectivities into absurdity
Joining on an expression or a function the planner has no stats for
Parameter sniffing in PL/pgSQL: a generic plan built for an unknown parameter; `SET plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan`
Data skew — one customer_id owns 90% of rows, but the plan was costed for the average
Ballooning table bloat makes reltuples and relpages lie about real size; VACUUM FULL or pg_repack to reset
Fix order: ANALYZE first, then extended stats, then indexes, then rewrite the query, and only then reach for hints
`enable_nestloop = off` etc. are diagnostic tools, not fixes — they prove which plan you wanted, then you go make the planner want it
pg_hint_plan extension for real hints when you genuinely cannot make the planner see it
`join_collapse_limit` / `from_collapse_limit` (both 8) — above that many tables, the planner stops exhaustively searching join orders
auto_explain module logs plans for slow queries in production, where you cannot re-run them by hand

chapters.title: Reading Real Plans: Worked Diagnoses
points: Step 1: find the node with the largest actual time × loops, not the largest cost
Step 2: check that node's rows estimate against its actual — that is where the plan broke
Step 3: look at BUFFERS — shared read means it went to disk, shared hit means it came from cache
Exclusive vs inclusive time: a node's `actual time` INCLUDES all its children; subtract to get self-time
Example — Nested Loop with `loops=48000`: real cost is 48000 × 0.03ms = 1.4s hidden in a node whose per-loop time looks trivial
Example — `Rows Removed by Filter: 4900000` on a Seq Scan: needs an index on the filtered column
Example — `Sort Method: external merge Disk: 180MB`: raise work_mem or add an index that supplies the order
Example — `Batches: 16` on a Hash node: the hash table spilled; the build side was underestimated
Example — Index Only Scan with `Heap Fetches: 890000`: VACUUM the table to refresh the visibility map
Example — `Workers Planned: 4 Workers Launched: 0`: worker pool exhausted by other queries
`Rows Removed by Join Filter` — a non-equi join condition being evaluated as a filter after the join
`Rows Removed by Index Recheck` — lossy bitmap pages costing real CPU
Trigger time is reported separately after the plan and is not included in node times
Use explain.depesz.com or explain.dalibo.com to visualize; they highlight estimate/actual mismatches automatically
Always run the query twice — the first run measures cold cache, the second measures the plan

chapters.title: Trade-offs, Comparisons, and Tuning Levers
points: Scan comparison — Seq: O(pages), sequential IO, no index maintenance; Index: O(log n + k) with random IO; Bitmap: index cost plus sequential-order heap reads
Join comparison — Nested Loop: O(N×M) or O(N log M) indexed, no memory; Hash: O(N+M), needs work_mem; Merge: O(N log N + M log M) unless pre-sorted, low memory
Index Only Scan is the only scan that avoids touching the heap — worth designing schemas around
Every index you add speeds reads and taxes every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE plus VACUUM time
Composite index column order: equality columns first, then range, then ORDER BY columns
Partial index (`WHERE status = 'active'`) can be a fraction of the size and stays hot in cache
work_mem: too low means disk sorts and hash batches; too high means an OOM when connections × nodes multiply
random_page_cost 4.0 → 1.1 on SSD is usually the single highest-leverage planner setting change
effective_cache_size should be roughly 50-75% of system RAM — it is a hint, it allocates nothing
default_statistics_target 100 → 500 on skewed columns costs ANALYZE time, buys accurate selectivity
Query rewrites that unlock better plans: EXISTS instead of IN on large subqueries, LATERAL instead of a correlated scalar subquery, avoiding functions on the indexed column
OFFSET N pagination scans and discards N rows — keyset pagination (`WHERE id > last_id`) stays constant time
Denormalize or add a materialized view when no plan can be fast enough; refresh cost is the trade
Partitioning helps only if the partition key is in the WHERE clause — otherwise you scan every partition
Measure with pg_stat_statements to find WHICH query to EXPLAIN; EXPLAIN answers why, pg_stat_statements answers where

chapters.title: Field Checklist and Summary
points: Standard invocation: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE, SETTINGS, FORMAT TEXT) <query>;`
The one-line summary of the whole discipline: find the node where estimated rows and actual rows diverge most
Cost is the planner's opinion; actual time is the truth — EXPLAIN alone shows only the opinion
Remember loops: actual time and actual rows are per-loop averages, always multiply
Triage order: pg_stat_statements to find the query, EXPLAIN ANALYZE BUFFERS to find the node, pg_stats to find the bad estimate
Fix ladder, cheapest first: ANALYZE → extended statistics → raise per-column statistics target → index → query rewrite → config change → hint
Never leave `enable_*` settings off in production — they are a debugging flashlight, not a repair
Scan cheat sheet: <1% of rows use Index, 1-10% use Bitmap, >10% use Seq
Join cheat sheet: tiny outer + indexed inner use Nested Loop, big equality use Hash, both sorted use Merge
Red flag list: Batches > 1, Sort Method external, lossy Heap Blocks, high Heap Fetches, Rows Removed by Filter in the millions, loops in the thousands
Always ANALYZE after a bulk load, restore, or major data shift — before you benchmark anything
Test on production-sized data; a plan that is right for 1,000 rows is often wrong for 10,000,000
auto_explain with log_min_duration captures the slow plans you cannot reproduce interactively
EXPLAIN in a transaction with ROLLBACK to safely analyze INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE
The planner is not your adversary — it is a cost model running on statistics; give it better statistics and it makes better choices
